summary: The note describes student-led health and wellness campaigns in Greenfield schools that began in September 2023, driven by students and educators concerned about youth mental and physical health after the pandemic. Initiatives include wellness weeks, a mental health speaker series, a student garden with cooking classes, a tech-based fitness program, and social media outreach. Early results show higher attendance and health knowledge, though funding shortages, systemic resistance and misinformation remain challenges.
one_line: Greenfield students and educators launched multi-school health and wellness campaigns in fall 2023 covering mental health, nutrition, fitness and online outreach, with early successes and ongoing obstacles.
key_facts: The student-led health and wellness campaigns in Greenfield began on September 15, 2023, with the official launch of interconnected projects on September 25, 2023.
Caroline Hayes, a senior at Greenfield High, cited alarming rates of stress, anxiety, and obesity among her peers as the initial spark for the campaign.
David Gomez, a health educator, said "It's time that we bridge the gap between knowledge and action."
Thompson Middle School students ran a "Well-Being Week" on nutrition, mindfulness and physical activity, led by eighth-grader Mia Zheng, who organized a schoolwide Zumba event.
Greenfield High set up peer support networks with help from local therapists and counselors, and began the "Speak Your Mind" speaker series on October 3rd.
Laura Henderson leads the nutrition project at Maplewood High, which includes a student-tended garden to teach about sustainable food sources.
Cooking classes and budget-friendly meal planning sessions have been offered on Saturdays since September 30th.
James Peterson, a phys-ed teacher and coach at Valley Forge High, created a customizable fitness program that uses technology to track students' progress in real time.
Peterson's fitness program kicked off on September 28th with a school-wide fitness fair and emphasizes inclusivity and personal goals over competition.
Erik Nguyen, a high school senior, manages the districtwide campaign's social media accounts, and students across the country have commented wanting to start similar campaigns.
Early successes include surging event attendance and district surveys showing a marked increase in students' knowledge and engagement with health topics.
Challenges include funding shortages, systemic resistance to adding new programs to the school day, and internet misinformation.
Marissa Glen, a teacher, and Jamal Parker, a social worker, remain committed; Parker said "the most important work isn't in the launching, but in the sustaining."
